The supercritical generalized KdV equation: Global well-posedness in the energy space and below Thanks: The second author was partially supported by CNPq/Brazil.

Luiz G. Farah Address: ICEx, Universidade Federal de Minas Gerais, Av. Antônio Carlos, 6627, Caixa Postal 702, 30123-970, Belo Horizonte-MG, Brazil Email address: lgfarah@gmail.com , Felipe Linares Address: IMPA, Estrada Dona Castorina 110, CEP 22460-320, Rio de Janeiro, RJ, Brazil. Email address: linares@impa.br and Ademir Pastor Address: IMECC-UNICAMP, Rua Sérgio Buarque de Holanda, 651, 13083-859, Campinas-SP, Brazil Email address: apastor@ime.unicamp.br
Abstract.

We consider the generalized Korteweg-de Vries (gKdV) equation ∂tu+∂x3u+μ​∂x(uk+1)=0\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u+\mu\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})=0, where k≥5k\geq 5 is an integer number and μ=±1\mu=\pm 1. In the focusing case (μ=1\mu=1), we show that if the initial data u0u_{0} belongs to H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) and satisfies E​(u0)sk​M​(u0)1−sk<E​(Q)sk​M​(Q)1−skE(u_{0})^{s_{k}}M(u_{0})^{1-s_{k}}<E(Q)^{s_{k}}M(Q)^{1-s_{k}}, E⁡(u0)≥0E(u_{0})\geq 0, and ‖∂xu0‖L2sk​‖u0‖L21−sk<‖∂xQ‖L2sk​‖Q‖L21−sk\|\partial_{x}u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{s_{k}}\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{1-s_{k}}<\|\partial_{x}Q\|_{L^{2}}^{s_{k}}\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{1-s_{k}}, where M⁡(u)M(u) and E⁡(u)E(u) are the mass and energy, then the corresponding solution is global in H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}). Here, sk=(k−4)2​ks_{k}=\frac{(k-4)}{2k} and QQ is the ground state solution corresponding to the gKdV equation. In the defocusing case (μ=−1\mu=-1), if kk is even, we prove that the Cauchy problem is globally well-posed in the Sobolev spaces Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}), s>4​(k−1)5​ks>\frac{4(k-1)}{5k}.

1. Introduction

Consider the Initial Value Problem (IVP) associated with the supercritical generalized Korteweg-de Vries (gKdV) equation, i.e.,

{∂tu+∂x3u+μ∂x(uk+1)=0,x∈ℝ,t>0,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u+\mu\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})=0,\;\;x\in\mathbb{R},\;t>0,\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\end{cases} (1.1)

where μ=±1\mu=\pm 1.

Local well-posedness of the Cauchy problem (1.1) (with k≥1k\geq 1) has been studied by many authors in recent years. We refer the reader to Kenig, Ponce and Vega [17], [18] for a complete set of sharp results.

Our main interest here is on global well-posedness. Let us briefly recall the best results available in the literature. For k=1k=1 and k=2k=2, global well-posedness was established by Colliander, Keel, Staffilani, Takaoka, and Tao [6] for data, respectively, in Hs(ℝ),s>−3/4H^{s}(\mathbb{R}),s>-3/4 and Hs​(ℝ),s>1/4H^{s}(\mathbb{R}),s>1/4, and by Guo [12] for data, respectively, in H−3/4(ℝ)H^{-3/4}(\mathbb{R}) and H1/4​(ℝ)H^{1/4}(\mathbb{R}). These results show to be sharp in view of the work of Kenig, Ponce, and Vega [19] (see also [1], [4], [27]).

The case k=3k=3 was dealt with by Grünrock, Panthee, and Silva [10], where the authors showed global well-posedness in Hs(ℝ),s>−1/42H^{s}(\mathbb{R}),s>-1/42. It should be pointed out that for k=3k=3, Tao [26] established a local existence result in H˙−16​(ℝ)\dot{H}^{-\frac{1}{6}}(\mathbb{R}), the critical (scale-invariant) space, therefore for small data the solutions extend globally. For recent progress in this case we refer Koch and Marzuola [20]. Under “sharp smallness condition”, the critical case k=4k=4 was studied by Fonseca, Linares, and Ponce in [9]. There it was established global well-posedness in Hs​(ℝ),s>3/4H^{s}(\mathbb{R}),s>3/4. Farah [8] used the I-method of [6], to further lower the regularity of the initial data to s>3/5s>3/5. Recently, Miao, Shao, Wu, and Xu [24], improved the latter result to initial data in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}), s>6/13s>6/13. Their method of proof combines the I-method with a multilinear correction analysis. For k=4k=4, Kenig, Ponce and Vega [17] showed local well-posedness for data in L2L^{2} the critical space in this case which for small data yield global solutions. Finally, we should mention that for k=4k=4, Merle [23] and Martel and Merle [22] proved the existence of real-valued solutions of (1.1) in H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) corresponding to data in u0∈H1​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) with ‖u0‖L2>‖Q‖L2\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}>\|Q\|_{L^{2}} that blow-up. For k>4k>4 it is an outstanding open problem.

As far as we are concerned, for k≥5k\geq 5, no global results below the energy space are available. Not even a precise description of the conditions to obtain H1H^{1} global solutions. These facts motivate the present study.

To start with the local results, using a scaling argument let us motivate what should be the Sobolev spaces to studying (1.1). Note if uu is a solution of (1.1), then, for any λ>0\lambda>0, uλ​(x,t)=λ2/k​u​(λ​x,λ3​t)u_{\lambda}(x,t)=\lambda^{2/k}u(\lambda x,\lambda^{3}t) is also a solution with initial data uλ​(x,0)=λ2/k​u0​(λ​x)u_{\lambda}(x,0)=\lambda^{2/k}u_{0}(\lambda x). Moreover,

‖uλ​(⋅,0)‖H˙s=λs+2/k−1/2​‖u0‖H˙s.\|u_{\lambda}(\cdot,0)\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}=\lambda^{s+2/k-1/2}\|u_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}.

Thus, for each kk fixed, the scale-invariant Sobolev space is H˙sk\dot{H}^{s_{k}}, sk=1/2−2/ks_{k}=1/2-2/k. Therefore, the natural Sobolev spaces to studying (1.1) are Hs{H}^{s}, s>sk=1/2−2/ks>s_{k}=1/2-2/k. Actually, this question has already been addressed by Kenig, Ponce, and Vega [17]. More precisely, they show the following.

Theorem 1.1.

Let k>4k>4 and s>sk=(k−4)/2​ks>s_{k}=(k-4)/2k. Then for any u0∈Hs​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) there exist T=T⁡(‖u0‖Hs)>0T=T(\|u_{0}\|_{H^{s}})>0 (with T⁡(ρ,s)→0T(\rho;s)\to 0 as ρ→0\rho\to 0) and a unique strong solution u⁡(⋅)u(\cdot) of the IVP (1.1) satisfying:

u∈C⁡([−T,T]:Hs​(ℝ)),u\in C([-T,T]:H^{s}(\mathbb{R})), (1.2)
‖u‖Lx5​LT10+‖Dxs​u‖Lx5​LT10<∞\|u\|_{L^{5}_{x}L^{10}_{T}}+\|D^{s}_{x}u\|_{L^{5}_{x}L^{10}_{T}}<\infty (1.3)
‖ux‖Lx∞​LT2+‖Dxs​ux‖Lx∞​LT2<∞,\|u_{x}\|_{L^{\infty}_{x}L^{2}_{T}}+\|D^{s}_{x}u_{x}\|_{L^{\infty}_{x}L^{2}_{T}}<\infty, (1.4)

and

‖Dtγk​Dxαk​Dtβk​u‖Lxpk​LTqk<∞\|D^{\gamma_{k}}_{t}D^{\alpha_{k}}_{x}D^{\beta_{k}}_{t}u\|_{L^{p_{k}}_{x}L^{q_{k}}_{T}}<\infty (1.5)

where

αk=110−25​k,βk=310−65​k,γk=γk​(s)=s−sk3\alpha_{k}=\frac{1}{10}-\frac{2}{5k},\qquad\beta_{k}=\frac{3}{10}-\frac{6}{5k},\qquad\gamma_{k}=\gamma_{k}(s)=\frac{s-s_{k}}{3} (1.6)
1pk=25​k+110,1qk=310−45​k.\frac{1}{p_{k}}=\frac{2}{5k}+\frac{1}{10},\qquad\frac{1}{q_{k}}=\frac{3}{10}-\frac{4}{5k}. (1.7)

Furthermore, given T′∈(0,T)T^{\prime}\in(0,T) there exists a neighborhood VV of u0u_{0} in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) such that the map u0↦u~​(t)u_{0}\mapsto\tilde{u}(t) from VV into the class defined by (1.2)-(1.4) with T′T^{\prime} instead of TT is smooth.

The method to prove Theorem 1.1 combines smoothing effects and Strichartz-type estimates together with the Banach contraction principle. As a matter of fact, the original theorem stated in [17] differs slightly in the functional spaces. Here, we will give a skech of the proof of Theorem 1.1 in this functional spaces setting.

Remark 1.2.

It should be observed that in [17] the authors also showed a local result for initial data in H˙sk​(ℝ)\dot{H}^{s_{k}}(\mathbb{R}), sks_{k} as above, but T=T⁡(u0)T=T(u_{0}), that is, the existence time TT depends on u0u_{0} itself and not on ‖u0‖H˙sk\|u_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{s_{k}}} (see also [1]) and that this is global if ‖u0‖H˙sk≤ck\|u_{0}\|_{\dot{H}^{s_{k}}}\leq c_{k} for real or complex-valued data.

Once Theorem 1.1 is established, a natural question presents itself: can the real solutions be extended globally-in-time? Such a question has mathematical and physical interest and it has been widely studied in the past few years.

By observing that the flow of the gKdV equation is conserved by the quantities:

M​a​s​s≡M⁡(u⁡(t))=∫u2​(t)​𝑑xMass\equiv M(u(t))=\int u^{2}(t)\,dx (1.8)

and

E​n​e​r​g​y≡E⁡(u⁡(t))=12​∫(∂xu)2​(t)​𝑑x−μk+2​∫uk+2​(t)​𝑑x,Energy\equiv E(u(t))=\frac{1}{2}\int(\partial_{x}u)^{2}(t)\;dx-\frac{\mu}{k+2}\int u^{k+2}(t)\;dx,\\ (1.9)

one can partially answer this question for solutions in H1​(ℝ)H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) if the initial data is small. Indeed, the quantities MM and EE allows us to obtain a priori estimates as follow: Using MM we can control ‖u⁡(t)‖L2\|u(t)\|_{L^{2}}. In order to control ‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L2\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}, we use EE by writing

‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L22=2​E​(u0)+2​μk+2​∫uk+2​(t)​𝑑x.\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=2E(u_{0})+\frac{2\mu}{k+2}\int u^{k+2}(t)\;dx. (1.10)

The Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality yields

∫uk+2​(t)​𝑑x≤c∥∂xu(t)∥L2θ⁡(k+2)∥u(t)∥L2(1−θ)​(k+2),θ=k2​(k+2),=c​‖u0‖L2(k+4)/2​‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L2k/2.\begin{split}\int u^{k+2}(t)\;dx&\leq c\,\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{\theta(k+2)}\|u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{(1-\theta)(k+2)},\quad\theta=\frac{k}{2(k+2)},\\ &=c\,\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{(k+4)/2}\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{k/2}.\end{split} (1.11)

From (1.10) and (1.11) it follows that

‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L22≤2​E​(u0)+2​ck+2​‖u0‖L2(k+4)/2​‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L2k/2.\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}\leq 2E(u_{0})+\frac{2c}{k+2}\,\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{(k+4)/2}\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{k/2}. (1.12)

Now let X⁡(t)=‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L22X(t)=\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{2}, for t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T) (TT given by Theorem 1.1). Since k>4k>4 the inequality (1.12) can be written as

X⁡(t)≤2​E​(u0)+2​ck+2​‖u0‖L2(k+4)/2​X​(t)1+ϵ,ϵ>0,X(t)\leq 2E(u_{0})+\frac{2c}{k+2}\,\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{(k+4)/2}X(t)^{1+\epsilon},\quad\epsilon>0, (1.13)

or

X⁡(t)−c⁡(k,‖u0‖L2)​X​(t)1+ϵ≤2​E​(u0).X(t)-c(k,\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}})\,X(t)^{1+\epsilon}\leq 2E(u_{0}). (1.14)

Thus if 0≤2​E​(u0)0\leq 2E(u_{0}) is not too large one can guarantee the existence of 0<β1<β20<\beta_{1}<\beta_{2} where the inequality (1.14) holds in the intervals [0,β1][0,\beta_{1}] and [β2,∞)[\beta_{2},\infty). By continuity if we have X⁡(0)∈[0,β1]X(0)\in[0,\beta_{1}], X⁡(t)X(t) will remain there for t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T). Hence ‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L2\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}} will be bound for t∈(0,T)t\in(0,T) and we can apply the local result to extend the solution. The argument works if the initial data is small enough, i.e., ‖u0‖H1\|u_{0}\|_{H^{1}} is sufficiently small to satisfy the conditions along the previous argument.

Note that the case where μ=−1\mu=-1 and kk even is, in some sense, special. Indeed, since kk is even we have ∫uk+2​(x,t)​𝑑x>0\int u^{k+2}(x,t)dx>0, for all t>0t>0, which implies

‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L22≲E⁡(u)​(t).\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|^{2}_{L^{2}}\lesssim E(u)(t).

Therefore, we have an a priori bound for ‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L2\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}} which, together with mass conservation (1.8) and local theory, implies global well-posedness without any smallness condition.

The above discussion can be summarized in the following theorem (see also [17, Theorem 2.15]).

Theorem 1.3.

Let k>4k>4 and s>sk=(k−4)/2​ks>s_{k}=(k-4)/2k. Then

  • (a)

    if μ=±1\mu=\pm 1, there exists δk>0\delta_{k}>0 such that for any u0∈H1u_{0}\in H^{1} with

    ‖u0‖H1<δk\|u_{0}\|_{H^{1}}<\delta_{k}

    there exists a unique strong solution u⁡(⋅)u(\cdot) of the IVP (1.1) satisfying

    u∈C⁡(ℝ:H1​(ℝ))∩L∞​(ℝ:H1​(ℝ)).u\in C(\mathbb{R}:H^{1}(\mathbb{R}))\cap L^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}:H^{1}(\mathbb{R})).
  • (b)

    if μ=−1\mu=-1 and kk is even then the same statement is true without any smallness assumption on the initial data.

We have two main goals in this paper. The first one is to make precise the H1H^{1}-size of the initial data (in the preceding argument) to construct global H1H^{1} solutions when μ=1\mu=1 or μ=−1\mu=-1 and kk odd. The second one is to loosen the regularity requirements on the initial data which ensure global-in-time solutions for the IVP (1.1) when μ=−1\mu=-1 and kk even. Below we also explain why we cannot apply the same method when μ=1\mu=1 or μ=−1\mu=-1 and kk odd (see Remark 5.9).

We consider first the focusing case μ=1\mu=1 or the defocusing case μ=−1\mu=-1 with kk odd. As explained above, it is not clear how large is the size of the initial data in H1H^{1} to obtain global solutions. The next theorem shows us how small the initial data should be.

Theorem 1.4.

Let u0∈H1​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}). Let k>4k>4 and sk=(k−4)/2​ks_{k}=(k-4)/2k. Suppose that

E​(u0)sk​M​(u0)1−sk<E​(Q)sk​M​(Q)1−sk,E⁡(u0)≥0.E(u_{0})^{s_{k}}M(u_{0})^{1-s_{k}}<E(Q)^{s_{k}}M(Q)^{1-s_{k}},\,\,\,E(u_{0})\geq 0. (1.15)

If

‖∂xu0‖L2sk​‖u0‖L21−sk<‖∂xQ‖L2sk​‖Q‖L21−sk,\|\partial_{x}u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{s_{k}}\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{1-s_{k}}<\|\partial_{x}Q\|_{L^{2}}^{s_{k}}\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{1-s_{k}}, (1.16)

then for any tt as long as the solution exists,

‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L2sk​‖u0‖L21−sk=‖∂xu⁡(t)‖L2sk​‖u⁡(t)‖L21−sk<‖∂xQ‖L2sk​‖Q‖L21−sk,\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{s_{k}}\|u_{0}\|_{L^{2}}^{1-s_{k}}=\|\partial_{x}u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{s_{k}}\|u(t)\|_{L^{2}}^{1-s_{k}}<\|\partial_{x}Q\|_{L^{2}}^{s_{k}}\|Q\|_{L^{2}}^{1-s_{k}}, (1.17)

where QQ is unique positive radial solution of the elliptic equation

Δ​Q−Q+Qk+1=0.\Delta Q-Q+Q^{k+1}=0.

This in turn implies that H1H^{1} solutions exist globally in time.

To prove Theorem 1.4, we follow closely the arguments in Holmer and Roudenko [13] which were inspired by those introduced by Kenig and Merle [15].

Next we consider the defocusing case μ=−1\mu=-1 with kk even. Our main result is the following.

Theorem 1.5.

Let μ=−1\mu=-1 and assume that kk is even. Let u0∈Hs​(ℝ),s>4​(k−1)5​ku_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}),s>\frac{4(k-1)}{5k}. Then, the local solution in Theorem 1.1 can be extended to any time interval. Moreover, for all T>0T>0, the solution satisfies

supt∈[0,T]{‖u⁡(t)‖Hs2}≤C​(1+T)(1+4/k)​(1−s)5​s−4​(k−1)/k+,\sup_{t\in[0,T]}\left\{\|u(t)\|^{2}_{H^{s}}\right\}\leq C(1+T)^{\frac{(1+4/k)(1-s)}{5s-4(k-1)/k}+}, (1.18)

where the constant CC depends only on ss and ‖u0‖Hs\|u_{0}\|_{H^{s}}.

Remark 1.6.

Note that when k=4k=4 we recover the result proved in Farah [8].

Here we use the approach introduced by Colliander, Keel, Staffilani, Takaoka and Tao in [5], the so-called II-method. We also explain why the refined approach introduced by the same authors in [6], cannot be used to improve our global result stated in Theorem 1.5 (see Proposition 5.1).

Note that when u0∈Hs​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) with s<1s<1 in (1.1), the energy (1.9) could be infinite, and so the conservation law (1.9) is meaningless. To overcome this difficulty, by following the II-method scheme, we introduce a modified energy functional which is also defined for less regular functions. Unfortunately, this new functional is not strictly conserved, but we can show that it is almost conserved in time. When one is able to control its growth in time explicitly this allows to iterate a modified local existence theorem to continue the solution to any time TT.

The plan of this paper is as follows. In the next section we introduce some notation and preliminaries. In Section 3 we prove Theorem 1.1. Next, in Section , we show Theorem 1.4. The result of global well-posedness in Theorem 1.5 is proved in Section 5.

2. Notation and Preliminaries

with the usual modifications when q=∞q=\infty or r=∞r=\infty. The Lxr​LtqL^{r}_{x}L^{q}_{t} norm is similarly defined.

f^​(ξ)=∫ℝe−i​x​ξ​f​(x)​𝑑x\hat{f}(\xi)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-ix\xi}f(x)dx

and the space-time Fourier transform of u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) by

u~​(ξ,τ)=∫ℝ∫ℝe−i⁡(x​ξ+t​τ)​u​(x,t)​𝑑t​𝑑x.\widetilde{u}(\xi,\tau)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}e^{-i(x\xi+t\tau)}u(x,t)dtdx.

Note that the derivative ∂x\partial_{x} is conjugated to multiplication by i​ξi\xi by the Fourier transform.

The set of Schwartz functions is represented by 𝒮⁡(ℝ)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}). We shall also define DsD^{s} and JsJ^{s} to be, respectively, the Fourier multipliers with symbols |ξ|s|\xi|^{s} and ⟨ξ⟩s=(1+|ξ|)s\langle\xi\rangle^{s}=(1+|\xi|)^{s}. ‖F‖Xs,b​(ℝ×ℝ)=‖⟨τ−ξ3⟩b​⟨ξ⟩s​F~‖Lξ,τ2.\|F\|_{X_{s,b}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R})}=\|\langle\tau-\xi^{3}\rangle^{b}\langle\xi\rangle^{s}\widetilde{F}\|_{L^{2}_{\xi,\tau}}.

‖u‖Xs,b​(I×ℝ)=inf{‖w‖Xs,b​(ℝ×ℝ):w⁡(t)=u⁡(t)​ on ​I}.\|u\|_{X_{s,b}(I\times\mathbb{R})}=\inf\left\{\|w\|_{X_{s,b}(\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R})}:w(t)=u(t)\textrm{ on }I\right\}.

Let us introduce now some useful lemmas and inequalities. In what follows, U⁡(t)U(t) denotes the group associated with the linear KdV equation, that is, for any u0u_{0}, U⁡(t)​u0U(t)u_{0} is the solution of the linear problem

{∂tu+∂x3u=0,x∈ℝ,t∈ℝ,u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x).\begin{cases}\partial_{t}u+\partial_{x}^{3}u=0,\;\;x\in\mathbb{R},\;t\in\mathbb{R},\\ u(x,0)=u_{0}(x).\end{cases} (2.19)

We begin by recalling the results necessary to prove Theorem 1.1.

Lemma 2.1.

The following inequalities hold.

  • (i)

    If u0∈Lx2u_{0}\in L^{2}_{x}, then

We now give some useful notation for multilinear expressions. If n≥2n\geq 2 is an even integer, we define a (spatial) nn-multiplier to be any function Mn​(ξ1,…,ξn)M_{n}(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{n}) on the hyperplane

Γn≡{(ξ1,…,ξn)∈ℝn:ξ1+⋯+ξn=0},\Gamma_{n}\equiv\{(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{n}:\xi_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{n}=0\},

which we endow with the standard measure δ⁡(ξ1+⋯+ξn)\delta(\xi_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{n}), where δ\delta is the Dirac delta.

If MnM_{n} is an nn-multiplier and f1,…,fnf_{1},\dots,f_{n} are functions on ℝ\mathbb{R}, we define the nn-linear functional Λn​(Mn,f1,…,fn)\Lambda_{n}(M_{n};f_{1},\dots,f_{n}) by

Λn​(Mn,f1,…,fn)=∫ΓnMn​(ξ1,…,ξn)​∏j=1nfj^​(ξj).\Lambda_{n}(M_{n};f_{1},\dots,f_{n})=\int_{\Gamma_{n}}M_{n}(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{n})\prod_{j=1}^{n}\widehat{f_{j}}(\xi_{j}).

We will often apply Λn\Lambda_{n} to nn copies of the same function uu in which case the dependence upon uu may be suppressed in the notation: Λn​(Mn,u,…,u)\Lambda_{n}(M_{n};u,\dots,u) may simply be written as Λn​(Mn)\Lambda_{n}(M_{n}).

If MnM_{n} is symmetric, so does the nn-linear functional Λn​(Mn)\Lambda_{n}(M_{n}).

As an example, suppose that uu is an ℝ\mathbb{R}-valued function. By Plancherel, we can rewrite the energy (1.9) in terms of nn-linear functionals as

E⁡(u⁡(t))=−12​Λ2​(ξ1​ξ2)−μk+2​Λk+2​(1).\displaystyle E(u(t))=-\dfrac{1}{2}\Lambda_{2}(\xi_{1}\xi_{2})-\dfrac{\mu}{k+2}\Lambda_{k+2}(1).

The time derivative of a symmetric nn-linear functional can be calculated explicitly if we assume that the function uu satisfies a particular PDE. The following statement may be directly verified by using the generalized KdV equation (1.1).

Proposition 2.8.

Suppose u satisfies the generalized KdV equation (1.1) and that MnM_{n} is a symmetric JJ-multiplier. Then

dd​t​ΛJ​(MJ)=Λn​(MJ​αJ)−i​J​μ​ΛJ+k​(Mn​(ξ1,…,ξJ−1,ξJ+⋯+ξJ+k)​(ξJ+⋯+ξJ+k)),\dfrac{d}{dt}\Lambda_{J}(M_{J})\!\!=\!\!\Lambda_{n}(M_{J}\alpha_{J})-iJ\mu\Lambda_{J+k}(M_{n}(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{J-1},\xi_{J}+\cdots+\xi_{J+k})(\xi_{J}+\cdots+\xi_{J+k})), (2.29)

where αn≡i⁡(ξ13+⋯+ξJ3)\alpha_{n}\equiv i(\xi_{1}^{3}+\cdots+\xi_{J}^{3}).

In this section, we intend to show Theorem 1.4. We begin by recalling the classical result obtained by Nagy [25] (see also Weinstein [28]), regarding the best constant of the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality (1.11).

Let k>0k>0, then the Gagliardo-Nirenberg inequality

‖u‖Lk+2​(ℝ)k+2≤Koptk+2​‖∇u‖L2​(ℝ)k2​‖u‖L2​(ℝ)2+k2,\|u\|_{L^{k+2}(\mathbb{R})}^{k+2}\leq K_{\rm opt}^{k+2}\,\|\nabla u\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}^{\frac{k}{2}}\|u\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R})}^{2+\frac{k}{2}}, (4.36)

5. Global well-posedness in HsH^{s}, s<1s<1: μ=−1\mu=-1 and kk even

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.5. As we mentioned in the introduction, we follow the “almost conservation law” scheme introduce in [5]–[7].

5.1. Modified energy functional

To start with, we introduced a substitute notion of “energy” that could be defined for less regular functions and that has very low increment in time. Given s<1s<1 and a parameter N≫1N\gg 1, define a multiplier operator IN:Hs→H1I_{N}:H^{s}\rightarrow H^{1} such that

IN​f​(ξ)^≡mN​(ξ)​f^​(ξ),\widehat{I_{N}f(\xi)}\equiv m_{N}(\xi)\widehat{f}(\xi),

where the multiplier mN​(ξ)m_{N}(\xi) is the nondecreasing in |ξ||\xi|, smooth and radially symmetric function defined as

mN​(ξ)={1, if |ξ|≤N,(N|ξ|)1−s, if |ξ|≥2N.\displaystyle m_{N}(\xi)=\left\{\begin{array}[]{ll }1&,\textrm{ if }|\xi|\leq N,\\ \left(\dfrac{N}{|\xi|}\right)^{1-s}&,\textrm{ if }|\xi|\geq 2N.\end{array}\right.

To simplify the notation, we omit the dependence of NN in INI_{N} and denote it only by II. Note that the operator II is smoothing of order 1−s1-s. Indeed we have

‖u‖Xs0,b0≤c​‖I​u‖Xs0+1−s,b0≤c​N1−s​‖u‖Xs0,b0,\|u\|_{X_{s_{0},b_{0}}}\leq c\|Iu\|_{X_{s_{0}+1-s,b_{0}}}\leq cN^{1-s}\|u\|_{X_{s_{0},b_{0}}}, (5.46)

for any s0,b0∈ℝs_{0},b_{0}\in\mathbb{R}.

Our substitute energy will be defined by E1​(u)=E​(I​u)E^{1}(u)=E(Iu). Obviously this energy makes sense even if uu is only in Hs​(ℝ)H^{s}(\mathbb{R}). Thus, in terms of nn-linear functionals we have

E1​(u)=−12​Λ2​(m1​ξ1​m2​ξ2)−μk+2​Λk+2​(m1​…​mk+2),E^{1}(u)=-\dfrac{1}{2}\Lambda_{2}(m_{1}\xi_{1}m_{2}\xi_{2})-\dfrac{\mu}{k+2}\Lambda_{k+2}(m_{1}\dots m_{k+2}), (5.47)

where mj=m⁡(ξj)m_{j}=m(\xi_{j}).

We can think about E1​(u)E^{1}(u) as the first generation of a family of modified energies. One can also define the second energy

E2​(u)=−12​Λ2​(m1​ξ1​m2​ξ2)−μk+2​Λk+2​(Mk+2​(ξ1,…,ξk+2)),E^{2}(u)=-\dfrac{1}{2}\Lambda_{2}(m_{1}\xi_{1}m_{2}\xi_{2})-\dfrac{\mu}{k+2}\Lambda_{k+2}(M_{k+2}(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{k+2})), (5.48)

where Mk+2M_{k+2} is an arbitrarily symmetric (k+2)(k+2)-multiplier.

Thus, using the derivation law (2.29), we obtain

dd​t​E2​(u)=−12​Λ2​(m1​ξ1​m2​ξ2​α2)+μ​ik+2​Λk+2​((m12​ξ13+⋯+mk+22​ξk+23)−Mk+2​(ξ13+⋯+ξk+23))+μ2​i​Λ2​k+2​(Mk+2​(ξ1,…,ξk+1,ξk+2+⋯+ξ2​k+2)​(ξk+2+⋯+ξ2​k+2)),\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt}E^{2}(u)&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\Lambda_{2}(m_{1}\xi_{1}m_{2}\xi_{2}\alpha_{2})\\ &\quad+\dfrac{\mu i}{k+2}\Lambda_{k+2}((m_{1}^{2}\xi_{1}^{3}+\dots+m_{k+2}^{2}\xi_{k+2}^{3})-M_{k+2}(\xi_{1}^{3}+\dots+\xi_{k+2}^{3}))\\ &\quad+\mu^{2}i\Lambda_{2k+2}(M_{k+2}(\xi_{1},\dots,\xi_{k+1},\xi_{k+2}+\cdots+\xi_{2k+2})(\xi_{k+2}+\cdots+\xi_{2k+2})),\end{split}

where we have used the identity ξ1+⋯+ξ6=0\xi_{1}+\cdots+\xi_{6}=0 and symmetrizing.

Note that picking

we can force Λk+2\Lambda_{k+2} to be zero. Unfortunately the multiplier Mk+2M_{k+2} is not well defined in the set Γk+2\Gamma_{k+2}. Proposition 5.1.

Therefore, throughout this section we work only with the first modified energy (5.47). Again, using the derivation law (2.29) and symmetrizing, we have

dd​t​E1​(u)=−12​Λ2​(m1​ξ1​m2​ξ2​(ξ13+ξ23))+μ​ik+2​Λk+2​((m12​ξ13+⋯+mk+22​ξk+23)−m1​…​mk+2​(ξ13+⋯+ξk+23))+μ2​i​Λ2​k+2​(m1​…​mk+1​m​(ξk+2+⋯+ξ2​k+2)​(ξk+2+⋯+ξ2​k+2)).\begin{split}\frac{d}{dt}E^{1}(u)&=-\dfrac{1}{2}\Lambda_{2}(m_{1}\xi_{1}m_{2}\xi_{2}(\xi_{1}^{3}+\xi_{2}^{3}))\\ &+\dfrac{\mu i}{k+2}\Lambda_{k+2}((m_{1}^{2}\xi_{1}^{3}+\dots+m_{k+2}^{2}\xi_{k+2}^{3})-m_{1}\dots m_{k+2}(\xi_{1}^{3}+\dots+\xi_{k+2}^{3}))\\ &+\mu^{2}i\Lambda_{2k+2}(m_{1}\dots m_{k+1}m(\xi_{k+2}+\cdots+\xi_{2k+2})(\xi_{k+2}+\cdots+\xi_{2k+2})).\end{split}

As one particular instance of the above computations and the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we have

=μ​ik+2​∫0tΛk+2​((m12​ξ13+⋯+mk+22​ξk+23)−m1​…​mk+2​(ξ13+…+ξk+23))​(t′)​d​t′+μ2i∫0tΛ2​k+2(m1…mk+1m(ξk+2+⋯+ξ2​k+2)(ξk+2+⋯+ξ2​k+2))(t′)dt′.\begin{split}=&\dfrac{\mu i}{k+2}\int_{0}^{t}\Lambda_{k+2}((m_{1}^{2}\xi_{1}^{3}+\dots+m_{k+2}^{2}\xi_{k+2}^{3})-m_{1}\dots m_{k+2}(\xi_{1}^{3}+\!\dots\!+\xi_{k+2}^{3}))(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}\\ &+\mu^{2}i\int_{0}^{t}\Lambda_{2k+2}(m_{1}\dots m_{k+1}m(\xi_{k+2}+\cdots+\xi_{2k+2})(\xi_{k+2}+\cdots+\xi_{2k+2}))(t^{\prime})dt^{\prime}.\end{split}

Most of our arguments here consist in showing that the quantity E1​(u)E^{1}(u) is almost conserved in time.

5.2. Almost conservation law

This subsection presents a detailed analysis of the expression (5.49). The analysis identifies some cancelations in the pointwise upper bound of some multipliers depending on the relative size of the frequencies involved. Our aim is to prove the following almost conservation property.

Proposition 5.3.

Let s>1/2s>1/2, N≫1N\gg 1 and u∈Hs​(ℝ)u\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) be a solution of (1.1) on [T,T+δ][T,T+\delta] such that I​u∈H1​(ℝ)Iu\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}). Then the following estimate holds

|E1​(u)​(T+δ)−E1​(u)​(T)|≲N−2+​(‖I​u‖X1,12+δk+2+‖I​u‖X1,12+δ2​k+2).\left|E^{1}(u)(T+\delta)-E^{1}(u)(T)\right|\lesssim N^{-2+}\left(\left\|Iu\right\|_{X^{\delta}_{1,\frac{1}{2}+}}^{k+2}+\left\|Iu\right\|_{X^{\delta}_{1,\frac{1}{2}+}}^{2k+2}\right). (5.50)

=(k+2)∫∗(m⁡(ξ2+⋯+ξk+2)m(ξ2)⋯m(ξk+2)−1)ξ13I​u​(ξ1)^⋯I​u​(ξk+2)^,=(k+2)\int_{\ast}\left(\frac{m(\xi_{2}+\cdots+\xi_{k+2})}{m(\xi_{2})\cdots m(\xi_{k+2})}-1\right)\xi_{1}^{3}\widehat{{Iu(\xi_{1})}}\cdots\widehat{Iu(\xi_{k+2})},

5.3. Proof of Theorem 1.5

Before proceeding to the proof of Theorem 1.5 we will first establish local well-posedness for the generalized KdV equation (1.1) in the Bourgain spaces Xs,bX_{s,b}. As in Theorem 1.1, by the Duhamel’s principle, we need to find a solution for the following integral equation

u⁡(t)=U⁡(t)​u0+∫0tU⁡(t−s)​∂x(uk+1)​(s)​𝑑s.u(t)=U(t)u_{0}+\int^{t}_{0}U(t-s)\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})(s)ds.

The proof proceeds by the usual fixed point argument. By well-known linear estimates, we have for all s>sks>s_{k}

‖u‖Xs,1/2+I\displaystyle\left\|u\right\|_{X_{s,1/2+}^{I}} =\displaystyle= ‖U⁡(t)​u0+∫0tU⁡(t−s)​∂x(uk+1)​(s)​𝑑s‖Xs,1/2+I\displaystyle\left\|U(t)u_{0}+\int^{t}_{0}U(t-s)\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})(s)ds\right\|_{X_{s,1/2+}^{I}} (5.53)
≲\displaystyle\lesssim ‖u0‖Xs,1/2+I+Tε‖∂x(uk+1)‖Xs,−1/2++I,\displaystyle\left\|u_{0}\right\|_{X_{s,1/2+}^{I}}+T^{\varepsilon}\left\|\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})\right\|_{X_{s,-1/2++}^{I}}, (5.54)

for sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0.

Thus, the crucial nonlinear estimate for the local existence is given in the following lemma.

Lemma 5.5.

For s>sk=(k−4)/2​ks>s_{k}=(k-4)/2k we have

‖∂x(uk+1)‖Xs,−12++≲‖u‖Xs,12+k+1.\|\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})\|_{X_{s,-\frac{1}{2}++}}\lesssim\|u\|^{k+1}_{X_{s,\frac{1}{2}+}}. (5.55)
Proof.

By the fractional Leibniz rule in Lemma 2.6, inequality (2.21), and Hölder inequality, we obtain

‖∂x(uk+1)‖Xs,−12++=‖Js​∂x(uk+1)‖X0,−12++≲‖Js​∂x(uk+1)‖Lx5/4+​Lt10/9+≲‖Js​(uk)‖Lxp1+​Ltq1+​‖∂xu‖Lxp2​Ltq2+‖uk‖Lx5/4+​Lt5/2+​‖Js​∂xu‖Lx∞​Lt2≲‖uk−1‖Lx5​k/4​(k−1)+​Lt5​k/2​(k−1)+​‖Js​u‖Lxp3​Ltq3​‖∂xu‖Lxp2​Ltq2+‖u‖Lx5​k/4​Lt5​k/2k−1​‖u‖Lx5​k/4+​Lt5​k/2+​‖Js​∂xu‖Lx∞​Lt2,\begin{split}\|\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})\|_{X_{s,-\frac{1}{2}++}}&=\|J^{s}\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})\|_{X_{0,-\frac{1}{2}++}}\lesssim\|J^{s}\partial_{x}(u^{k+1})\|_{L_{x}^{5/4+}L_{t}^{10/9+}}\\ &\lesssim\|J^{s}(u^{k})\|_{L_{x}^{p_{1}+}L_{t}^{q_{1}+}}\|\partial_{x}u\|_{L_{x}^{p_{2}}L_{t}^{q_{2}}}+\|u^{k}\|_{L_{x}^{5/4+}L_{t}^{5/2+}}\|J^{s}\partial_{x}u\|_{L_{x}^{\infty}L_{t}^{2}}\\ &\lesssim\|u^{k-1}\|_{L_{x}^{5k/4(k-1)+}L_{t}^{5k/2(k-1)+}}\|J^{s}u\|_{L_{x}^{p_{3}}L_{t}^{q_{3}}}\|\partial_{x}u\|_{L_{x}^{p_{2}}L_{t}^{q_{2}}}\\ &+\|u\|^{k-1}_{L_{x}^{5k/4}L_{t}^{5k/2}}\|u\|_{L_{x}^{5k/4+}L_{t}^{5k/2+}}\|J^{s}\partial_{x}u\|_{L_{x}^{\infty}L_{t}^{2}},\end{split}

where p2p_{2} and p3p_{3} are defined as in (2.27).

Therefore, an application of inequalities (2.25) and (2.26) followed by inequalities (2.23) and (2.24) yield the desired estimate (5.55). ∎

Remark 5.6.

As a consequence, one can recover all the well known range of existence for the local theory in terms of the Xs,bX_{s,b} spaces.

Next, we consider the following modified equation

{Iut+Iux​x​x+I(uk+1)x=0,x∈ℝ,t>0,I​u​(x,0)=I​u0​(x).\displaystyle\left\{\begin{array}[]{l}Iu_{t}+Iu_{xxx}+I(u^{k+1})_{x}=0,\hskip 7.22743ptx\in\mathbb{R},\,t>0,\\ Iu(x,0)=Iu_{0}(x).\end{array}\right.

Clearly if I​u∈H1​(ℝ)Iu\in H^{1}(\mathbb{R}) is a solution of (5.3), then u∈Hs​(ℝ)u\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) is a solution of (1.1) in the same time interval. Therefore, we need to prove that, in fact, the above modified equation has a global solution.

Applying the interpolation lemma (see [7], Lemma 12.1) to (5.55), we obtain

∥∂xI(uk+1)∥X1,−1/2++≲∥Iu∥X1,1/2+k+1.\|\partial_{x}I(u^{k+1})\|_{X_{1,-1/2++}}\lesssim\|Iu\|^{k+1}_{X_{1,1/2+}}.

where the implicit constant is independent of NN. Now, standard arguments invoking the contraction-mapping principle give the following variant local well-posedness result.

Theorem 5.7.

Assume sk<s<1s_{k}<s<1. Let u0∈Hs​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) be given. Then there exists a positive number δ\delta such that the IVP (5.3) has a unique local solution I​u∈C⁡([0,δ]:H1​(ℝ))Iu\in C([0,\delta]:H^{1}(\mathbb{R})) such that

‖I​u‖X1,12+δ≲‖I​u0‖H1.\|Iu\|_{X^{\delta}_{1,\frac{1}{2}+}}\lesssim\|Iu_{0}\|_{H^{1}}. (5.59)

Moreover, the existence time can be estimated by

δ∼1‖I​u0‖H1σ,\delta\sim\dfrac{1}{\|Iu_{0}\|^{\sigma}_{H^{1}}},

where σ>0\sigma>0.

Now, we have all tools to prove our global result stated in Theorem 1.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.5.

Let u0∈Hs​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}) with sk<s<1s_{k}<s<1. Our goal is to construct a solution to (5.3) (and therefore to (1.1)) on an arbitrary time interval [0,T][0,T]. Remark 5.9.

It is not clear how to apply the II-method when μ=1\mu=1 or μ=−1\mu=-1 and kk odd. In this case, we may not have inequality (5.60). Therefore, to perform the interactions explained above we need to verify the hypotheses of Theorem 1.4 for the modified solution I​u​(t)Iu(t) at each step. However, the only available estimate in the homogeneous H1H^{1}-Sobolev space is the following

‖∂xI​ut‖L2≲N1−s​‖u⁡(t)‖H˙s.\|\partial_{x}Iu_{t}\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim N^{1-s}\|u(t)\|_{\dot{H}^{s}}.

Since, at the end of the argument we need to take NN large, we cannot satisfy the inequalities (1.15)-(1.17) during all the interactions.
